feed.title: Towards A K-of-N Lightning Network Node

entry.title: Towards A K-of-N Lightning Network Node
entry.summary:
Revocation key management in secure multi-party computation (MPC) systems relies on each signer revealing their unique revocation key, derived from their personal revocation root key. The node then combines this revealed key with the public output from the MPC via an XOR operation, resulting in the true revocation key. This arrangement preserves the fundamental interaction pattern between the signer, or validator logic system (VLS), and the node itself: signers retain full control over when to release their revocation keys, ensuring that such release only occurs after local validation.
Operational modifications are minimal and localized primarily to the node’s implementation. Only the node is required to store a copy of the keyblob, eliminating the need to distribute keyblob fragments to signers for decryption purposes. Ciphertext efficiency offers a further benefit; ciphertexts produced in this scheme maintain parity in length with plaintexts. Traditional asymmetric encryption, as used in threshold cryptography, generally incurs overhead where the ciphertext exceeds the plaintext size. Since decrypting one revocation key at a time is both safer and more practical, avoiding batch decryption prevents the risk of lingering sensitive data—namely, unreleased future revocation keys—in memory or cache. Given that each revocation key is only 32 bytes, typical cryptographic overheads of 32 to 64 bytes become significant if applied per key, highlighting the value of achieving no expansion in ciphertext size.
A critical distinction arises when considering the use of MPC versus a trusted offline computer for key management. Trusted offline computers constrain node operation to a single entity, as only the operator can safely hold the private root revocation key. However, leveraging n-of-n MPC enables cooperative node operation among multiple independent entities. This approach allows several participants to pool their resources, collectively running what is termed a "nodelet"—each acting as a partial signer. Together, these nodelets form a robust Lightning Network (LN) node capable of competing with larger corporate-operated nodes. No single small entity would reasonably trust an external machine with exclusive access to the root revocation key, making MPC not just preferable but essential for such collaborative arrangements.
